title: Can Tech Simplify Pro Bono? — full episode transcript

author: Zachary Oswald · Linda Warren Seely

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: The source forecasts AI-supported self-service for routine legal matters and case-specific guidance for pro bono lawyers, with attorneys intervening as complexity rises. It does not assess whether automating junior work undermines expertise reproduction or propose deliberate apprenticeship reforms, so its position on the cluster’s principal proposition cannot be determined.

st.t: Service redesign: Resistance reflects incentives and identity
st.an: The source accepts legal AI as human-centred organisational change and extends the cluster with a concrete pro bono model: client-specific attorney preparation, continuing support, experimentation, leadership and human–technology collaboration. Its claims about greater participation and scale remain aspirational rather than measured.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts selective, human-led deployment and materially extends it with a concrete pro bono operating model: automate preparatory paperwork, preserve lawyer-client interaction, require lawyer review before chatbot responses are released, and secure judicial and cross-system collaboration. It also recognises accessibility limits, reinforcing that technology access alone is insufficient.

st.t: Justice augmentation: Activity exceeds proven access gains
st.an: The source aligns with the cluster’s augmentation framing by presenting existing technology as a way to support volunteer attorneys and scale pro bono assistance, rather than replace human legal work. It also reinforces the cluster’s evidentiary caution: the discussion identifies opportunities and projects but supplies no measured access or legal-outcome gains.

kp.k: AI and document automation accelerate expungement petition production
kp.d: Zachary Oswald describes an operating reentry workflow at Legal Aid of Middle Tennessee: a subscription ChatGPT model configured with classification rules processes criminal records into a spreadsheet, Excel holds the data, Zapier connects applications, and Gavel generates petitions. He reports producing 20 petitions in five minutes or less for dismissed or retired charges. Cat Moon stresses that generative AI is only one component alongside established automation tools; the transcript supplies practitioner-reported throughput rather than a comparative evaluation.
qs: We upload somebody’s criminal record, it creates for us then a spreadsheet based on rules that we’ve taught it to look for, what’s been dismissed versus what’s retired, what’s a diverted charge or what’s a conviction?

Then using Zapier, it takes the Excel sheet that we’ve got, throws that through Zapier, who then connects to Gavel, which is our document automation system, and it automatically generates those petitions.
we can generate those 20 petitions in five minutes or less just by grabbing the record from the internet, dropping into chat GPT back into Excel, zap over to gavel, those get printed.

kp.k: Established automation supports statewide self-service and representation backup
kp.d: Oswald argues that ordinary document automation, not only novel AI, meets unmet legal needs. He describes a Gavel-based Tennessee certificate-of-restoration process that translates plain-language answers into petitions, available to anyone in the state. He says almost 500,000 formerly incarcerated people could restore their civil rights if they knew the process, which involves courts, the Secretary of State and multiple paperwork layers. Partner organizations offer representation when users cannot proceed independently.
qs: There are almost 500,000 people that have lost their civil rights because they’ve been incarcerated who could get them restored if they knew the process to go through.
You have to go through the courts, then you have to go through the Secretary of State.
That is available for anybody in the state of Tennessee
So we’ve also got the representation backup for people who may not be able to do it pro se.

kp.k: Online debt resolution requires trust and accessible interfaces
kp.d: Linda Warren Seely reports high usage, easier settlements and considerable hospital savings from an Erlanger medical-debt online dispute-resolution platform, without numerical outcome measures. The asynchronous, text-based negotiation process permits a Rule 31 listed mediator to assist. She identifies initial distrust and difficulties for less technologically confident clients; involving the Hamilton County court system helped establish trust. Statewide and general sessions court expansion are aspirations, while mediator use of AI to generate options and strategies is described as a subject of discussion.
qs: the hospital has found that it has saved them considerable amounts of money and time and effort in collecting debts.
there’s the opportunity to bring in a rule 31 listed mediator to help the parties
they weren’t sure if they really should trust this.
But what we’ve been talking to the mediators about is using AI to generate options

kp.k: Proposed chatbot assistance retains volunteer lawyer verification
kp.d: Seely proposes adding chatbot-generated responses to Free Legal Answers, an existing asynchronous, text-based volunteer-lawyer service. Her proposed workflow requires lawyers to inspect and approve chatbot output before it reaches users. This is a recommendation for supervised assistance, not a claim that the service already uses autonomous AI advice.
qs: But it uses volunteer lawyers and I think personally that we ought to have a chat bot and then have the volunteer lawyers go back and take a look at what the chat bot says, and then if it gets a thumb up, thumbs up, then it goes out.

kp.k: Adoption and volunteer confidence constrain technology-enabled pro bono
kp.d: Seely identifies professional adoption as the hardest obstacle, citing lawyer anxiety about even Zoom hearings and uneven availability of electronic filing in Tennessee. Oswald similarly describes volunteers' anxiety about unfamiliar practice areas. He recommends tools, comparison of generated work and nearby legal-aid support to make participation less intimidating; Seely recommends demonstrations and learning to use existing technology.
qs: I think adoption on the part of the legal profession is the hardest thing, quite frankly.
there’s still some rural areas where there’s not electronic filing.
This is outside of their comfort zone. They do transactional law, they do construction law.
All you’re going to do is compare it. We’re going to be right beside you, and then you’re going to explain it to the next person.

kp.k: Automation redirects volunteer time toward meaningful client interaction
kp.d: Oswald argues that reducing paperwork lets volunteers spend more time with clients and experience their work as valuable. Seely illustrates this with a junior associate whose pro bono conservatorship provided her first opportunity to speak with a client, unlike the narrow assignments she received at a large firm. Moon frames improved human connection as a benefit of technology and suggests conversations could improve in quality; these are practitioner arguments and anecdotes, not measured effects.
qs: So if we can take the paperwork out of the process, or we can automate that to make it quicker so that they can spend more time talking to John Doe, to Jane Doe, who’s right in front of them, they’re going to feel like they actually accomplished something
So the associates, they’re just working on little tiny pieces of litigation or transactions. This was her first time to actually talk to a client

kp.k: Reported clinic outcomes support volunteer recruitment and retention
kp.d: Oswald reports that a Belmont clinic held two weeks before the conversation expunged 187 records and secured $531,000 in court-cost waivers in one day's work. He recommends communicating concrete accomplishments to volunteers so they recognize their contribution and return. These are reported clinic outcomes, not an estimate isolating AI's contribution or a financial return calculation.
qs: we expunged 187 records and had no, sorry, $531,000 in court cost waived in one day’s worth of work.
it’s something that you can feed to a pro bono attorney that gets them to come back because they realize that they actually contributed to changing people’s lives.

kp.k: Hybrid clinics expand access through judicial and organizational cooperation
kp.d: Oswald describes simultaneous Belmont and Tennessee Justice Center clinic sites, with judges serving clients in person and over video. He links the satellite option to transportation, parking, age and disability barriers, and says faster processing enabled expansion. Court-clerk assistance and judicial buy-in were important operational conditions. Moon draws the broader lesson that leadership and collaboration across institutions are necessary for these projects.
qs: we actually had a second site set up at the Tennessee Justice Center in North Nashville to allow people who had transportation issues.
the reason we were able to expand upon that again is because we had a product that allows us to expedite the process.
then turn immediately to the screen next to them and talk to our satellite site at the Tennessee Justice Center and go ahead and expunge records there.
So having buy-in from those judges was really, really excellent.

kp.k: Next projects target convictions and affordable focused research
kp.d: Oswald says the current priority is expanding the expungement tool to convictions, highlighting Tennessee's different treatment of convictions before 1985, from 1985 to 96 and after 96 as a complication. Seely wants focused AI legal-research assistance for lawyers across her firm's jurisdictions, using Tennessee landlord-tenant questions as an example. She presents affordability and whether she could build such a tool as unresolved constraints.
qs: Our focus right now is on expanding the current tool that we’re working on to include convictions.
that gets really complicated in Tennessee, depending on whether the conviction was before 1985 from 1985 to 96 after 96.
I want more legal research focus, and I know there’s stuff out there, I just don’t know if we can afford it or if I can build it.

kp.k: 2030 visions combine routine self-service and individualized lawyer guidance
kp.d: In response to Moon's hypothetical 2030 scenario of pervasive generative AI, Seely anticipates more people handling routine matters online, with lawyers assisting in complex cases and concentrating more on policy or large-scale litigation; she conditions this on professional adoption and court-system change. Oswald instead emphasizes individualized AI case manuals covering timelines, pleadings and pitfalls, extending general guides and continuing legal education to support unfamiliar pro bono work, realistic client expectations and volunteer confidence. These are aspirations under the host's scenario, not demonstrated capabilities or established forecasts.
qs: what I’d like to see is for people to be able to handle routine legal matters in a efficacious, expeditious fashion online using generative AI to both complete forms to get the forms in front of the right people, to get them approved.
we have to be willing to adopt those models and the court system has to be willing to change to let people do it that way.
here’s what the timeline looks like, here are the pleadings that you’re going to need to file. Here are the potential pitfalls that are going to come up.

That would be my dream is let’s continue doing what we’re doing, but let’s make it more focused on what the client’s needs and what the client’s going to be able to do so that we can teach the attorney how to do it specifically.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Oswald describes an operational AI-assisted expungement workflow and predicts individualized support for volunteer lawyers; Seely proposes lawyer-reviewed chatbots, AI-assisted mediation and research, and greater self-service for routine legal matters.
pts.d:
1. Zachary Oswald says his legal aid organization's workflow uses a subscription ChatGPT model configured with rules to extract and classify criminal-record information, followed by Excel, Zapier and Gavel to generate expungement petitions. He reports that it can produce 20 petitions in five minutes or less. This is a claim about an integrated AI and document-automation workflow, not ChatGPT alone.
2. Oswald argues that these tools reduce volunteer lawyers' anxiety about unfamiliar practice areas and remove paperwork so they can spend more time with clients. He describes lawyers comparing the generated work with support available, rather than an unsupervised replacement for lawyers. He also says the expedited process enabled the clinic to extend service to a remote satellite location.
3. Linda Warren Seely describes discussions with mediators about using AI to generate negotiation options and map strategies in an asynchronous medical-debt dispute-resolution service. Separately, she proposes a chatbot for Free Legal Answers whose answers would be reviewed and approved by volunteer lawyers before release. That chatbot is a proposal, not a reported deployment.
4. Seely wants a focused AI legal-research tool to condense state-specific material and guide pro bono lawyers, but presents this as a desired capability with affordability and buildability unresolved.
5. In the 2030 scenario, Seely predicts more self-represented litigants handling routine matters online with generative AI completing forms and helping move them through submission and approval. Lawyers would provide guidance or intervene in complex matters, and focus more on policy or large-scale litigation, using AI for pleadings and discovery.
6. In the same scenario, Oswald envisages generative AI producing individualized case manuals with timelines, required pleadings and potential pitfalls. He predicts this would prepare volunteer attorneys for court and client conversations, align expectations with achievable outcomes, and increase willingness to undertake pro bono work.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The principal evidence consists of practitioner accounts of a working system and clinic outcomes; proposed and future applications are supported by experience and reasoning rather than formal testing.
pts.d: Oswald gives a concrete description of the software stack and a practitioner-reported throughput figure of 20 petitions in five minutes or less, without providing a measured pre-automation baseline, accuracy results or an independent evaluation. He reports that the Belmont clinic, held two weeks before the conversation, expunged 187 records and secured $531,000 in court-cost waivers in one day. Those figures describe the clinic's combined work, including volunteers, court staff, judges and technology; the transcript does not isolate AI's contribution. Seely corroborates her participation at that clinic and work with its expungement process. Oswald's account of the satellite site supplies a concrete operational example of expanded reach. His claims about volunteer confidence, satisfaction and repeat participation draw on his pro bono experience and reasoning, not recruitment or retention statistics. Seely draws on extensive legal aid, dispute-resolution and pro bono experience. Her positive reports about medical-debt settlements and hospital savings concern the broader online dispute-resolution platform and should not be attributed specifically to AI. No evaluated implementation is supplied for her proposed lawyer-reviewed chatbot or focused research tool. Both speakers' 2030 accounts are aspirations and predictions, not measured findings.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The source distinguishes current expungement automation, near-term expansion and proposals, and a conditional 2030 vision; human support, legal complexity, adoption and court cooperation are recurring conditions.
pts.d: The expungement workflow is described as already operating at the time of the episode, supplied as 2024. The rapid-generation example concerns clients with dismissed or retired charges. Oswald says the current development priority is expansion to convictions, where Tennessee's differing legal requirements for convictions before 1985, from 1985 to 1996, and after 1996 create complexity. The account therefore does not claim that the existing workflow already handles all convictions. The mediator use is described as something being discussed; the Free Legal Answers chatbot and research tool are desired developments without deadlines. Seely expressly conditions chatbot release on lawyer approval. Oswald's present model retains lawyer comparison, organizational support and client explanation. Satellite delivery depended on court-clerk assistance and participating judges. The future predictions respond to a 2030 hypothetical in which generative AI is widely integrated; they are not unconditional forecasts of adoption. Seely limits unaided self-service primarily to routine matters, retains lawyers for complexity, and says both professional adoption and court-system change are necessary. She also identifies client trust and difficulty with text-based interaction as barriers in the existing online dispute-resolution setting, and lawyer adoption as a broader bottleneck.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claims concern access to justice and pro bono capacity: legal aid clients, self-represented people, volunteer lawyers, mediators and courts, rather than enterprise legal-market savings or lawyer headcount.
pts.d: People leaving incarceration and seeking expungement are the immediate beneficiaries of Oswald's AI-assisted workflow; clinic participants also obtained court-cost relief. The satellite clinic reached people facing transportation, parking, age-related or disability-related access barriers. Volunteer attorneys practicing outside their normal specialties are expected to gain confidence, reduce time spent preparing paperwork, and have more meaningful client contact. Legal aid organizations are positioned to support those volunteers and serve additional locations. Medical-debt mediators are potential users of AI-generated options and strategies; debtors and the hospital are the parties those proposals would serve. Users of Free Legal Answers would receive chatbot-assisted responses only after volunteer-lawyer verification under Seely's proposal. Her research-tool aspiration concerns lawyers working across the states where her firm has offices. In the 2030 vision, members of the public with routine legal needs would become more capable of self-representation, while lawyers would continue to handle complexity, guidance, policy and major litigation. Oswald's individualized guidance would support lawyers and clients rather than replace their relationship. The speakers do not quantify job displacement, fee changes or law-firm staffing effects.
